claims.text: The starting material is a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments within a Cu matrix.
A minor Ni addition can be localized at W–Cu interfaces during powder processing.
Localized interfacial Ni will induce formation of a W–Ni–Cu intermetallic phase.
Sintering at approximately 1100°C for 10–30 minutes under a controlled atmosphere is an applicable processing window.
The proposed composite is applicable in service up to approximately 900°C and an irradiation dose of about 10 dpa.
The Ni treatment will produce a continuous, thin W–Ni–Cu intermetallic layer at W–Cu interfaces.
The W–Ni–Cu intermetallic layer will bond W and Cu effectively.
The Ni-rich interlayer enhances interfacial wettability.
The Ni-rich interlayer acts as a diffusion barrier.
The diffusion-barrier effect reduces differential-diffusion-driven phase separation.
The Ni-rich interlayer prevents interfacial void nucleation.
Reduced phase separation and void nucleation stabilize the interface under thermal and irradiation stresses.
Interface stabilization minimizes interfacial thermal impedance.
Ni-treated W–Cu composites will have higher thermal conductivity than untreated W–Cu composites under the specified simulated service conditions.
Untreated W–Cu composites typically undergo phase separation under comparable heat and irradiation conditions.
Untreated W–Cu composites typically form interfacial voids under comparable heat and irradiation conditions.
Phase separation and interfacial voids reduce the thermal conductivity of untreated W–Cu composites.
The proposed material is relevant to joints between W-based plasma-facing components and Cu-based cooling systems.
Excessive or otherwise nonoptimal Ni-interlayer composition or thickness may compromise the intrinsic high thermal conductivity of the Cu matrix.
